key_points: Open-source self-evolving multi-agent framework with an AI-native game engine that turns natural language into fully playable 2D web games
Built on Claude Code & OpenAI Codex agent runtimes, Phaser-based 2D engine, Python 3.12+, Apache 2.0 license
From Pattern Recognition Laboratory, Nanjing University; technical report dated Aug 17, 2026; ~220 stars, 12 forks
Adversarial Agent Team of 8 specialized agents (orchestrator, designer, artist, architect, programmer, auditor, player, reviewer) that separates generation from review
AI-native engine represents project as structured text with schema validation, exposes frame-synchronous runtime control so agents play-test at their own pace
Training-free self-evolution distills accepted projects into reusable skeletons, verified modules, and collaboration contracts as project priors
Demos: Hollow Knight boss slice, Civilization prototype, KOF arcade fighter, dungeon roguelike, Fruit Ninja, Aniya Parkour, Pixel Sekiro, AI Werewolf party game
Editing scenarios: IP transfer, genre transfer, rule restructuring; roadmap adds Godot, Unity, and end-to-end 3D
A DIFFERENT project sharing the name: a 3D game engine designed for vibe coding
Declarative HTML-like syntax, ECS architecture with plugins, physics/rendering/player controls out of the box
Live demos on Hugging Face Spaces and JSFiddle; NPM package; uses Shallot for context management
Contrast: engine-focused (dylanebert) vs agent-team-focused (tettethu)
Vibe Voyager: browser space exploration game built in ~66 minutes by 35+ parallel AI agents using Claude Code subagent-driven development
8 planets, 34 missions, 5 mini-games, 10 Academy reference guides, ~14,400 lines of production TypeScript
Narrative mirrors arc from Karpathy's 'vibe coding' (2025) to 'agentic engineering' (2026)
Demonstrates parallel multi-agent game building but without the self-evolution or adversarial verification of VibeGame
GameDevBench: first benchmark for evaluating agents on game development tasks, set in the Godot engine
132 tasks (later 333) derived from web/video tutorials across gameplay logic, 2D/3D graphics, UI
Average solution requires over 3x the lines of code and file changes vs prior software benchmarks
Best agent solves only ~54.5% of tasks — agents still struggle with game development
VibeGame notes no benchmark yet targets JavaScript/Phaser end-to-end game generation
GameCraft-Bench: 140-task Godot benchmark from CUHK Shenzhen, Tencent Hunyuan, NUS, SJTU across 15 game genres
Claude Code Opus-4.7 tops leaderboard at 41.46%; GPT-5.5 at 39.49%; Kimi-K2.6 at 30.65%
Top agent still fails on content depth (39.48%) and art/presentation (36.86%) — the outputs most visible to players
Huge capability spread: DeepSeek-V4-Pro scored just 2.15%
Verification via replayed gameplay and rubric-guided multimodal judging

angles: The 'vibe coding' to 'agentic engineering' evolution: VibeGame moves from single-session chat to a persistent, self-evolving multi-agent team
Adversarial verification as the differentiator: separating generation from review (auditor static checks + player runtime play-testing) catches bugs single-agent pipelines miss
Frame-synchronous control lets agents play-test real-time games at their own pace — solving the 'millisecond game vs slow reasoning' mismatch
Training-free self-evolution: reusable skeletons and collaboration contracts mean each new game starts from a higher baseline without retraining
The benchmark gap: GameDevBench/GameCraft-Bench target Godot, but no benchmark yet covers JavaScript/Phaser end-to-end game generation — VibeGame fills an unmeasured niche
2D-to-3D roadmap and Godot/Unity support signal where prompt-to-game development is heading
Name collision warning: tettethu/VibeGame (agent framework) vs dylanebert/VibeGame (3D engine) are unrelated projects
